--- title: "SimulationStudy Class" description: "A streamlined guide using the SimulationStudy manager." number-sections: true --- Use the `SimulationStudy` manager to handle the entire lifecycle: storage, diagnostics, active refinement, analysis, and intelligent caching. ::: {.callout-note} In this tutorial, we will intentionally feed the study **"bad" data** (with a large gap in the input space) to demonstrate how the active learning module automatically identifies and fixes issues. We will also demonstrate how the new **Layered Caching** engine makes exploring multi-dimensional parameter spaces nearly instantaneous. ::: ## Setup, Generation & Smart Initialization {#sec-setup} We'll define a simulated physics function with heteroscedastic noise and generate an initial design containing a deliberate gap between 3mm and 7mm. Notice that we no longer need to explicitly define our input columns when creating the `SimulationStudy`; the manager will automatically infer them from the data! ::: {#75fb2cda .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import time from digiqual import SimulationStudy # --- Define the Physics --- def apply_physics(df): """Simulates a signal with quadratic trends and heteroscedastic noise.""" signal = ( 10.0 + (2.0 * df["Length"]) + (0.5 * df["Length"] ** 2) - (0.1 * np.abs(df["Angle"])) ) noise_scale = 0.5 + (1.5 * df["Roughness"]) noise = np.random.normal(loc=0, scale=noise_scale, size=len(df)) return signal + noise # --- Create Flawed Data (Gap between 3mm and 7mm) --- df1 = pd.DataFrame( { "Length": np.random.uniform(0.1, 3.0, 40), "Angle": np.random.uniform(-10, 10, 40), "Roughness": np.random.uniform(0, 0.5, 40), } ) df2 = pd.DataFrame( { "Length": np.random.uniform(7.0, 10.0, 40), "Angle": np.random.uniform(-10, 10, 40), "Roughness": np.random.uniform(0, 0.5, 40), } ) df_initial = pd.concat([df1, df2], ignore_index=True) df_initial["Signal"] = apply_physics(df_initial) # --- The NEW Smarter Initialization --- # 1. Initialize with a clean slate study = SimulationStudy() # 2. Add data: It automatically infers 'Length', 'Angle', 'Roughness' as inputs! study.add_data(df_initial, outcome_col="Signal", overwrite=True) # Test the UI Helper methods print(f"Inferred Inputs: {study.inputs}") threshold_defaults = study.get_data_summary("Signal") print(f"Auto-Threshold suggestion (Median Signal): {threshold_defaults['median']:.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Data initialized/overwritten. Total rows: 80 Inferred Inputs: ['Length', 'Angle', 'Roughness'] Auto-Threshold suggestion (Median Signal): 35.44 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip} ### Designing real experiments: `generate_lhs` Here we use random synthetic data. For real simulations, build the input design with `digiqual.sampling.generate_lhs(n, ranges)`, which gives a space-filling design you can run in order and stop early ([details](optimisation.qmd#sec-diagnostics)). ::: ## Diagnosis (Detecting the Issue) {#sec-diagnosis} We ask the `SimulationStudy` manager to diagnose the health of our experiment. ::: {.callout-warning} Because of our deliberate gap, we expect the diagnostic engine to flag the **Input Coverage** test as failed. The full list of tests and their default thresholds is in [Sampling & Diagnostics](optimisation.qmd#sec-diagnostics). ::: ::: {#441308e1 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Run the diagnostic tests study.diagnose() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Running validation... Validation passed. 80 valid rows ready. Checking sample sufficiency... ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Reliability Analysis & Layered Caching {#sec-reliability} With a validated dataset, we can now run the complete PoD pipeline. ::: {.callout-tip} The single `pod()` method runs the whole [Generalised PoD](generalised_pod.qmd) pipeline: - **Model Selection**: polynomial or Kriging, chosen by cross-validation with the one-standard-error rule - **Variance Modelling** and **Distribution Inference**: the changing scatter and its best-fitting error distribution - **Monte-Carlo Integration**: marginalising out nuisance variables (Uniform, or custom Normal, Lognormal or Weibull) - **Sobol Sensitivity Analysis**: total-order sensitivity indices for each input - **Bootstrapping**: confidence bounds (when `n_boot > 0`) The first call fits and caches all the models, so later calls that only change a slice or threshold are almost instant ([how the caching works](caching.qmd)). Progress messages are printed through Python's `logging` (the `"digiqual"` logger). To silence them, use `logging.getLogger("digiqual").setLevel(logging.WARNING)`. ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Why Configure Custom Nuisance Profiles? In the code snippet below, we pass `nuisance_dists={"Roughness": ("norm", (0.25, 0.08))}` to the `.pod()` engine instead of letting it default to a Uniform distribution. If we assume surface roughness is Uniformly distributed between its extreme bounds, the Monte Carlo integration treats an incredibly rough, worst-case surface as just as likely to occur as a nominal, well-machined surface. This would unnecessarily degrade our final Probability of Detection curve. By specifying a **Normal distribution** centered around the nominal design specification ($0.25$ with a standard deviation of $0.08$), `digiqual` samples coordinates that mirror real-world production distributions. This ensures your final calculated reliability curves represent field performance, rather than an unphysical worst-case scenario. ::: ::: {#analysis-run .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # --- RUN 1: Baseline Analysis --- # Expect this to take a moment as it trains models # and optimizes variance bandwidth. # We configure 'Roughness' with a custom Normal distribution: mean=0.25, std=0.08 t0 = time.time() results = study.pod( poi_col="Length", nuisance_col=["Roughness"], # Integrate over roughness slice_values={"Angle": 0.0}, # Hold Angle strictly at 0.0! threshold=34.0, n_boot=0, # Skipping bootstrap for the speed demonstration nuisance_dists={"Roughness": ("norm", (0.25, 0.08))}, ) print(f"Run 1 completed in: {time.time() - t0:.4f} seconds") # Access the calculated Sobol sensitivity indices for each input parameter print("Sobol Sensitivity Indices (Total Effect):") for var, val in results["sobol_indices"].items(): print(f" {var}: {val * 100:.1f}%") # --- RUN 2: Interactive Slicing --- # Changing the constant 'Angle' slice triggers # a Cache Hit for the model and variance! t1 = time.time() new_results = study.update_slice({"Angle": 5.0}) print(f"Run 2 completed in: {time.time() - t1:.4f} seconds (Near Instant!)") # update_slice() re-runs pod() with n_boot=0: the PoD curve without confidence # bounds, so there are no aX/Y values yet (they need the bootstrap, below). # Read the PoD of a 5 mm flaw off the curve instead. lengths = new_results["X_eval"].flatten() pod_5mm = np.interp(5.0, lengths, new_results["curves"]["pod"]) print(f"PoD of a 5 mm flaw at Angle 5.0: {pod_5mm:.3f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` --- Starting Reliability Analysis (PoIs: ['Length'] - Nuisance: ['Roughness']) --- -> Slicing surface at: {'Angle': 0.0} 1. PoD of a 5 mm flaw at Angle 5.0: 0.022 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#fig-results .cell layout-ncol='1' execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Visualise the results of the final active slice study.visualise() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Best Fitting Model (Statistics)](qs_class_files/figure-html/fig-results-output-1.png){#fig-results-1 width=942 height=519} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Signal Response Model (Physics)](qs_class_files/figure-html/fig-results-output-2.png){#fig-results-2 width=585 height=449} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Probability of Detection Curve (Reliability)](qs_class_files/figure-html/fig-results-output-3.png){#fig-results-3 width=589 height=449} ::: Reliability Analysis Results ::: ## Uncertainty Quantification & Threshold Sensitivity {#sec-uq} To calculate reliability indices with confidence intervals, we run the bootstrapping algorithm. Unlike traditional tools that compute only a single confidence interval (e.g., 95%), `digiqual` runs bootstrapping once to extract bounds for **multiple confidence levels** (50%, 90%, 95%, 99%) across standard target PoDs (50%, 90%, 95%, 99%) simultaneously. These are saved in the results dictionaries: - `results['ci_bounds']`: Maps confidence levels to lower/upper curves. - `results['reliability_table']`: Maps `(target_pod_percent, confidence_level)` tuples to their corresponding flaw sizing reliability indices (e.g., `a90/95`). The bootstrap below uses the same settings as Run 2, including the Normal distribution for `Roughness`. Leave out `nuisance_dists` and `Roughness` would be integrated uniformly instead, giving a different curve. ::: {#14c138f0 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # The PoD setup from Run 2, reused below settings = dict( poi_col="Length", nuisance_col=["Roughness"], slice_values={"Angle": 5.0}, nuisance_dists={"Roughness": ("norm", (0.25, 0.08))}, ) # Run the parallelised bootstrap to get multi-level confidence bounds t2 = time.time() uq_results = study.pod( **settings, threshold=34.0, n_boot=100, # Small value for quick demonstration n_jobs=-1, # All CPU cores except two (1 = a single core, same results) ) print(f"UQ Bootstrapping completed in: {time.time() - t2:.4f} seconds") # Access the custom reliability matrix values # Print the calculated a90/95 and a90/90 values a90_95 = uq_results["reliability_table"].get((90, 95)) a90_90 = uq_results["reliability_table"].get((90, 90)) print(f"a90/95: {a90_95:.3f} mm") print(f"a90/90: {a90_90:.3f} mm") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` --- Starting Reliability Analysis (PoIs: ['Length'] - Nuisance: ['Roughness']) --- -> Slicing surface at: {'Angle': 5.0} 1. Loading surrogate models from cache (Cache Hit)... -> Selected Model: Polynomial (Degree 2) 2. Loading Variance Model, Distribution & Sobol from cache (Cache Hit)... -> Smoothing Bandwidth: 1.2699 (input std devs) -> Selected Distribution: weibull_max 3. Loading PoD Curve from Individual Cache (Layer 3 Hit)... 4. Running Bootstrap (100 iterations on 10 cores)... -> [Bootstrap] Running 100 iterations on 10 worker core(s)... -> [Bootstrap Progress] Completed 50/100 iterations (50%)... -> [Bootstrap Progress] Completed 100/100 iterations (100%)... -> a90/95 Reliability Index: 5.483 --- Analysis Complete --- UQ Bootstrapping completed in: 11.1756 seconds a90/95: 5.483 mm a90/90: 5.463 mm ``` ::: ::: We can specify a custom `target_pod` and `confidence_level` when calling `visualise()` to draw and annotate the selected point. ::: {#fig-uq-results .cell layout-ncol='1' execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} study.visualise(target_pod=0.90, confidence_level=90) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Best Fitting Model (Statistics)](qs_class_files/figure-html/fig-uq-results-output-1.png){#fig-uq-results-1 width=942 height=519} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Signal Response Model (Physics)](qs_class_files/figure-html/fig-uq-results-output-2.png){#fig-uq-results-2 width=585 height=449} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![UQ Reliability S-curve with 90% Confidence Bounds for a 90% target PoD](qs_class_files/figure-html/fig-uq-results-output-3.png){#fig-uq-results-3 width=589 height=449} ::: Reliability Analysis Results ::: ### Threshold Sensitivity Plots {#sec-threshold-sensitivity} `compute_pod_spectrum()` takes the same settings as `pod()` and computes the PoD for 100 thresholds across the observed signal range in one pass, caching the result (Layer 4 in [Caching](caching.qmd)). Afterwards, `pod()` calls with those settings, `n_boot=0` and a threshold inside that range interpolate from it instead of integrating. It does not replace `study.pod_results`, so the bootstrap results above are kept. `plot_pod_vs_threshold()` then plots the spectrum for the current results, to show how the threshold affects PoD across defect sizes. The spectrum must have been computed with the same settings as those results. ::: {#cell-fig-sensitivity .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Generate the threshold spectrum for the bootstrap's settings (Layer 4 cache) spectrum = study.compute_pod_spectrum(**settings) print(f"{len(spectrum['thresholds'])} thresholds from {spectrum['thresholds'][0]:.1f} to {spectrum['thresholds'][-1]:.1f}") # Plot sensitivity curves _ = study.plot_pod_vs_threshold() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` --- Initiating Threshold Spectrum Generation --- --- Starting Reliability Analysis (PoIs: ['Length'] - Nuisance: ['Roughness']) --- -> Slicing surface at: {'Angle': 5.0} 1. Loading surrogate models from cache (Cache Hit)... -> Selected Model: Polynomial (Degree 2) 2. Loading Variance Model, Distribution & Sobol from cache (Cache Hit)... -> Smoothing Bandwidth: 1.2699 (input std devs) -> Selected Distribution: weibull_max 3. Integrating PoD Curve from Scratch (Cache Miss)... 4. Skipping Bootstrap (n_boot=0)... --- Analysis Complete --- 4. Computing PoD Spectrum for 100 thresholds (Layer 4 Cache Miss)... --- Spectrum Generation Complete --- 100 thresholds from 8.0 to 77.1 ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![PoD vs. Threshold Sensitivity Plot](qs_class_files/figure-html/fig-sensitivity-output-2.png){#fig-sensitivity width=758 height=566} ::: ::: ### The reliability matrix {#sec-reliability-matrix} `digiqual.pod.reliability_matrix()` arranges `reliability_table` as a table: one row per target PoD, one column per confidence level. With `as_text=True` the values are rounded and unreached targets read *Not Reached*; without it they stay numbers (NaN when not reached). ::: {#bbdf37ee .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} from digiqual.pod import reliability_matrix reliability_matrix(uq_results["reliability_table"], as_text=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## More Control {#sec-more-control} ### Fitting the model on its own: `fit_model()` {#sec-fit-model} `pod()` fits the model itself, but you can also fit it first, for example to check the chosen model before any PoD. `fit_model(model_override="auto", force_degree=None, bandwidth_ratio=None, progress_callback=None)` fits the surrogate (mean) model, the scatter (variance) model, the error distribution and the Sobol indices, all on every input. The result is cached and also stored in `study.model_results`, so a later `pod()` with the same model reuses it. ::: {#021ae415 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} fit = study.fit_model() # "auto": the cross-validation pick print("Model:", fit["model_key"], "| error distribution:", fit["dist_info"][0]) # Force a different model: model_override is "auto", "polynomial" or "kriging" fit_cubic = study.fit_model(model_override="polynomial", force_degree=3) print("Forced model:", fit_cubic["model_key"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1. Loading surrogate models from cache (Cache Hit)... -> Selected Model: Polynomial (Degree 2) 2. Loading Variance Model, Distribution & Sobol from cache (Cache Hit)... -> Smoothing Bandwidth: 1.2699 (input std devs) -> Selected Distribution: weibull_max Model: ('Polynomial', 2) | error distribution: weibull_max 1. Loading surrogate models from cache (Cache Hit)... -> Selected Model: Polynomial (Degree 3) 2. Fitting Variance Model & Inferring Distribution (Cache Miss)... -> Optimizing bandwidth via LOO-CV... -> Calculating Total-Order Sobol Indices... -> Smoothing Bandwidth: 1.2528 (input std devs) -> Selected Distribution: norm Forced model: ('Polynomial', 3) ``` ::: ::: To make `pod()` use a forced model, pass the same `model_override` and `force_degree` to it. ### Integration ranges and fitted distributions {#sec-nuisance} Integrated (nuisance) variables are sampled uniformly over their observed range unless you say otherwise: - `nuisance_dists` gives a variable a distribution, as a `(scipy_name, params)` pair. `digiqual.integration.estimate_nuisance_distribution(values, kind)` fits one to data, for each `kind` in `NUISANCE_DISTRIBUTIONS` (Uniform, Normal, Lognormal, Weibull). It returns `None` for Uniform, and raises a `ValueError` if the distribution can't be fitted (Lognormal and Weibull need positive values). - `nuisance_bounds` narrows the integration range, as `{column: (low, high)}`. Limits outside the observed data are clamped to it, because the model can't be trusted there. ::: {#366cad65 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} from digiqual.integration import NUISANCE_DISTRIBUTIONS, estimate_nuisance_distribution print("Available:", NUISANCE_DISTRIBUTIONS) roughness_dist = estimate_nuisance_distribution(study.clean_data["Roughness"], "Normal") print("Fitted Normal:", roughness_dist) bounded = study.pod( poi_col="Length", nuisance_col=["Roughness"], slice_values={"Angle": 0.0}, threshold=34.0, n_boot=0, nuisance_dists={"Roughness": roughness_dist}, nuisance_bounds={"Roughness": (0.1, 0.9)}, # 0.9 is beyond the data ) print("Integration range used:", bounded["nuisance_bounds"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Available: ('Uniform', 'Normal', 'Lognormal', 'Weibull') Fitted Normal: ('norm', (0.2575432052430568, 0.14559739368947036)) --- Starting Reliability Analysis (PoIs: ['Length'] - Nuisance: ['Roughness']) --- -> Slicing surface at: {'Angle': 0.0} 1. Loading surrogate models from cache (Cache Hit)... -> Selected Model: Polynomial (Degree 2) 2. Loading Variance Model, Distribution & Sobol from cache (Cache Hit)... -> Smoothing Bandwidth: 1.2699 (input std devs) -> Selected Distribution: weibull_max 3. Integrating PoD Curve from Scratch (Cache Miss)... 4. Skipping Bootstrap (n_boot=0)... --- Analysis Complete --- Integration range used: {'Roughness': (0.1, 0.4903000294468018)} ``` ::: ::: ### Progress callbacks {#sec-progress} `fit_model()` and `pod()` take a `progress_callback`, called as `(done, total)` or `(done, total, label)`: `fit_model()` while it cross-validates the candidate models (only the first, slow fit for a dataset), and `pod()` during the bootstrap. The app uses these for its progress panels. Progress messages also go to the `"digiqual"` logger. ::: {#0ea4e20f .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} def report(done, total, label=""): if done == total: print(f"Finished {total} bootstrap iterations") _ = study.pod(**settings, threshold=34.0, n_boot=20, progress_callback=report) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` --- Starting Reliability Analysis (PoIs: ['Length'] - Nuisance: ['Roughness']) --- -> Slicing surface at: {'Angle': 5.0} 1. Loading surrogate models from cache (Cache Hit)... -> Selected Model: Polynomial (Degree 2) 2. Loading Variance Model, Distribution & Sobol from cache (Cache Hit)... -> Smoothing Bandwidth: 1.2699 (input std devs) -> Selected Distribution: weibull_max 3. Loading PoD Curve from Individual Cache (Layer 3 Hit)... 4. Finished 20 bootstrap iterations -> a90/95 Reliability Index: 5.478 --- Analysis Complete --- ``` ::: ::: ### Reading results from a CSV: `digiqual.io` {#sec-io} `digiqual.io.read_results_csv(path)` reads a results file and cleans it exactly as the app does. The cleaning itself is `clean_columns(df)`, which returns the cleaned table, the names of the dropped text columns and the number of text cells turned into missing values: - column names are trimmed, spaces become underscores and other special characters are removed; - duplicate names are numbered (`Signal`, `Signal_1`); - text columns, and completely empty ones, are dropped; - stray text cells in a numeric column become missing values, so validation later drops those rows. ::: {#2a562152 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} from digiqual.io import clean_columns raw = pd.DataFrame({ "Crack Length (mm)": [1.0, 2.0, 3.0], "Operator": ["A", "B", "C"], "Signal": [0.5, "n/a", 1.4], "Signal ": [0.6, 0.9, 1.3], }) clean, dropped, n_bad = clean_columns(raw) print("Columns:", list(clean.columns)) print("Dropped text columns:", dropped, "| text cells made missing:", n_bad) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Columns: ['Crack_Length_mm', 'Signal', 'Signal_1'] Dropped text columns: ['Operator'] | text cells made missing: 1 ``` ::: ::: ## Appendix: Full Script {#sec-full-script} ::: {#analysis-full .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import time from digiqual import SimulationStudy # --- 1. Define the Physics --- def apply_physics(df): """Simulates a signal with quadratic trends and heteroscedastic noise.""" signal = ( 10.0 + (2.0 * df["Length"]) + (0.5 * df["Length"] ** 2) - (0.1 * np.abs(df["Angle"])) ) noise_scale = 0.5 + (1.5 * df["Roughness"]) noise = np.random.normal(loc=0, scale=noise_scale, size=len(df)) return signal + noise # --- 2. Create Flawed Data --- df1 = pd.DataFrame( { "Length": np.random.uniform(0.1, 3.0, 40), "Angle": np.random.uniform(-10, 10, 40), "Roughness": np.random.uniform(0, 0.5, 40), } ) df2 = pd.DataFrame( { "Length": np.random.uniform(7.0, 10.0, 40), "Angle": np.random.uniform(-10, 10, 40), "Roughness": np.random.uniform(0, 0.5, 40), } ) df_initial = pd.concat([df1, df2], ignore_index=True) df_initial["Signal"] = apply_physics(df_initial) # --- 3. Initialize & Ingest --- study = SimulationStudy() study.add_data(df_initial, outcome_col="Signal", overwrite=True) # --- 4. Diagnose & Refine --- study.diagnose() study.plot_collinearity() new_samples = study.refine(n_points=20) if not new_samples.empty: new_samples["Signal"] = apply_physics(new_samples) study.add_data(new_samples) # --- 5. Fast-Path Reliability Exploration (Caching) --- # Calculate the base physics model (n_boot=0) to prime Layers 1 and 2 study.pod(poi_col="Length", threshold=15.0, n_boot=0) # Generate a 100-threshold spectrum matrix (Layer 4 Cache) instantly spectrum = study.compute_pod_spectrum(poi_col="Length") print("Spectrum generated for thresholds:", spectrum["thresholds"][:3], "...") # Plot threshold sensitivity curves study.plot_pod_vs_threshold() # --- 6. Uncertainty Quantification (Bootstrapping) --- # Run the heavy, parallelised bootstrap to get multi-level Confidence Intervals # (n_jobs=-1 uses all CPU cores except two) results = study.pod(poi_col="Length", threshold=15.0, n_boot=100, n_jobs=-1) # Print specific reliability matrix values (e.g. a90/95) a90_95 = results["reliability_table"].get((90, 95)) print(f"a90/95: {a90_95:.2f}") # --- 7. Visualisation --- # Annotate target PoD of 90% and confidence level of 95% study.visualise(target_pod=0.90, confidence_level=95) ``` :::
